overview: Shoshoni is an older spelling of Shoshone. This broad map entry covers communities across the Great Basin and Rocky Mountains, rather than a single kingdom. Its outline combines regional homelands, while the dates mark imported map coverage. The examples below identify particular communities so that one family’s history does not become everybody’s story.

periods.title: Regional communities
periods.summary: Different bands organized life around local waters, plants, animals and seasonal travel.

periods.title: Encounters and increasing pressure
periods.summary: Expedition accounts describe skilled Lemhi Shoshone guides, fishers and makers; settlement later brought mounting conflict.

periods.title: Violence and reservation boundaries
periods.summary: The Bear River massacre and treaties reshaped different Shoshone communities in sharply different ways.

periods.title: Community persistence
periods.summary: Land campaigns, oral historians and language projects carried community knowledge into new institutions.

items.text: Some regional bands were identified by foods strongly associated with their home areas, such as salmon or pine nuts. These names reflected local knowledge and relationships. The Northwestern Band’s history describes many smaller family groups, a useful reminder that this enormous map shape never had one royal capital.

In the Bear River and Cache Valley region, winter camps used dense willows and brush for protection from wind and snow. The Northwestern Band also describes nearby hot springs, fish and game. Choosing a campsite meant knowing a whole neighborhood of useful places, not simply finding an empty patch of ground.

In August 1805, expedition observers described Lemhi Shoshone fishing barriers made from poles and willows. Basket traps caught fish moving in both directions. Narrow basket ends could be untied to remove the catch: river engineering with a built-in opening for dinner.

Cameahwait explained the landscape to Meriwether Lewis by drawing rivers on the ground and making small mounds to represent mountains. His account warned of difficult routes. In this 1805 meeting, the visitor’s notebook depended on a local expert’s knowledge of the country.

Lewis also recorded Shoshone women making and repairing his party’s moccasins. He described hide robes that served as daytime clothing and nighttime covers. Those August 1805 observations preserve a glimpse of the skilled work that kept travelers shod and warm.

Yellowstone archaeologists associate a pottery tradition called Intermountain Ware with Shoshone presence roughly seven centuries ago. Fragments of cooking vessels can preserve traces of everyday activities long after their owners’ camps have disappeared. This is a regional archaeological clue within a much longer history of people using Yellowstone.

Eastern Shoshone leader Washakie worked through a period of expanding settlement and military pressure. The tribe’s history connects treaties in 1863 and 1868 with the eventual Wind River reservation. Washakie favored a place familiar as a wintering area, tying political negotiations to lived knowledge of the landscape.

On January 29, 1863, United States troops attacked Northwestern Shoshone families at Bear River. The massacre devastated this community. Its later history includes the return of land: the Northwestern Band purchased a substantial part of the massacre site in 2018, strengthening its role in caring for the place.

Mae Timbimboo Parry began writing down elders’ histories while she was still in high school. Her grandfather had survived Bear River as a child. She later challenged accounts calling the massacre a battle, helping bring community testimony into the public history of the event.

For Timbisha Shoshone families in Death Valley, houses built in the 1930s came without indoor plumbing or electricity, and residents shared a water tap. Their seasonal travel out of the heat later became an excuse for officials to destroy empty houses. A home could be occupied seasonally and still be somebody’s home.

Timbisha women including Pauline Esteves and Barbara Durham helped lead the struggle for a secure homeland. Federal recognition in 1983 and the Timbisha Shoshone Homeland Act in 2000 were major steps. This southern community has its own history, rather than serving as a stand-in for every Shoshone nation.

A recorded Duck Valley expression is “Hakanni e?”, translated “How are you?” in the University of Utah’s Shoshoni dictionary. Its entry credits Crum, Crum and Dayley’s 2002 work. This is an attested modern spelling of a spoken expression, offered with its regional attribution.

The Shoshoni Talking Dictionary grew through collaboration with communities and young learners. Its history describes work with Ely Shoshone beginning in 2008 and later recordings involving youth and elders. A digital dictionary can carry pronunciation as well as print, preserving differences between speakers and communities.

At Fort Hall, the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes’ language and culture program describes archives supporting family history, land claims and language learning. Shoshone and Bannock instruction are identified separately. Family records can therefore help both a child asking about relatives and a nation documenting its rights.

ending.text: The map’s 1783 cutoff is not an ending for Shoshone peoples. Distinct communities and governments continue, including Eastern Shoshone, Northwestern Shoshone and Timbisha Shoshone. Their histories include losses of land and lives, but also continuing language work, leadership and claims to home.
